setting: A short lecture in a world history class about how the Silk Road connected regions through trade.
narrator_intro: Listen to part of a talk in a world history class.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: When people hear “Silk Road,” they often imagine one paved highway. It was actually a network of routes.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: For centuries, caravans moved goods between East Asia, Central Asia, the Middle East, and parts of Europe.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Silk was famous, but traders also carried spices, glass, metals, horses, and paper-making ideas.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Cities such as Samarkand became busy hubs where merchants rested, exchanged currency, and shared news.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: The routes were dangerous: deserts, mountain passes, and bandits made travel slow and expensive.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Because of that cost, long-distance trade favored high-value, lightweight goods rather than bulk grain.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Ideas traveled too—religions, artistic styles, and technologies moved along with the caravans.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: The network declined as maritime trade grew and political control along the land routes shifted.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Still, historians study the Silk Road to understand early globalization—not just fashion or fabric.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Next time we'll compare land routes with Indian Ocean sea trade in the same period.

narrator_outro: Now get ready to answer the questions.

questions.narrator_text: What is the talk mainly about?

options.A: How to manufacture modern silk clothing
options.B: How Silk Road routes connected regions through trade and ideas
options.C: Why Europe banned all Asian imports
options.D: How to navigate a desert with GPS

questions.explanation: The professor describes the Silk Road as a network moving goods and ideas across regions.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing A—silk is mentioned as a famous good, not as a manufacturing lesson.

questions.narrator_text: According to the professor, what was the Silk Road?

options.A: A single paved highway from China to Rome
options.B: A network of routes across multiple regions
options.C: A railroad built in the nineteenth century
options.D: A river used only for fishing

questions.explanation: He says people imagine one highway, but it was actually a network of routes.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing A—that is the misconception he corrects.

questions.narrator_text: Why did long-distance trade favor high-value, lightweight goods?

options.A: Because farmers refused to grow grain
options.B: Because travel was slow, dangerous, and expensive
options.C: Because silk could not be folded
options.D: Because ships were illegal on land routes

questions.explanation: Deserts, mountains, and bandits made travel slow and expensive, so traders preferred high-value lightweight goods.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing A—grain is mentioned as an example of bulk goods that were less favored, not a farmer refusal.

questions.narrator_text: Besides goods, what else moved along the routes?

options.B: Ideas such as religions, artistic styles, and technologies

questions.explanation: He says ideas traveled too—religions, artistic styles, and technologies moved with the caravans.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing A—military equipment is not what he lists as traveling with the caravans.
